blocks.md: Logarithms turn multiplication into addition, and that makes them the natural language of growth. A change in the log of a variable is, for small changes, its percentage change; differences in logs add up over time and are symmetric, which percentages are not. Growth rates of products and powers become simple sums and multiples. And the elasticity — the percentage response of one variable to another — is just the slope in logs.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: Almost every growth rate, wage gap and elasticity in economics is computed or interpreted through logs.
Natural log rules: $\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b$, $\ln(a/b) = \ln a - \ln b$, $\ln a^k = k\ln a$, $e^{\ln a} = a$.
A change in a log **is** a proportional change.
The approximation is the first Taylor term ([Taylor Series Approximation](note:taylor-series-approximation)). A log gap of 0.67 means $e^{0.67} - 1 = 95\%$ higher, not 67%.

| Property | Log difference | Percentage change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Additive over time | $\ln(y_2/y_0) = \ln(y_1/y_0) + \ln(y_2/y_1)$ | Compounds instead |
| Symmetric | Up then down by 0.1 returns to start | +10% then −10% does not |
| Scale-free | Unchanged by units or inflation | Same |

If $y_t$ grows continuously at rate $g$, $y_t = y_0e^{gt}$ and $d\ln y/dt = g$. Doubling time is $\ln 2/g \approx 70/(g\text{ in }\%)$ — the **rule of 70**. At 2% the exact answer is $\ln 2/0.02 = 34.66$ years (with annual compounding, $\ln 2/\ln 1.02 = 35.0$).

sections.heading: Growth rates of products, ratios and powers

blocks.md: Because logs turn products into sums, growth rates (log differences) combine linearly:

These are exact for log differences and continuous growth, and approximations for discrete percentage changes: if $X$ grows 3%, $X^{0.5}$ grows 1.489% (rule: 1.5%); if $X$ grows 2% and $Y$ 3%, $XY$ grows 5.06% (rule: 5%). Dropping the cross term $g_Xg_Y$ is a first-order [Taylor Series Approximation](note:taylor-series-approximation).
In a log-log relationship the elasticity is the slope.

- **Econometrics**: interpreting log-linear, linear-log and log-log models ([Functional Forms and Elasticities](note:functional-forms-and-elasticities)); [Box-Cox and Power Transformations](note:box-cox-and-power-transformations) with $\lambda = 0$.
- **Inequality / labor**: [Log Wage Gap](note:log-wage-gap), [Percentile Ratios](note:percentile-ratios), [Variance of Log Income](note:variance-of-log-income), the log-linear relative wage equation in the [Canonical Model of the Skill Premium](note:canonical-model-of-the-skill-premium), and $-1/\sigma$ as an elasticity ([Elasticity of Substitution](note:elasticity-of-substitution)).
- **Macro**: growth accounting ([Multivariable Chain Rule](note:multivariable-chain-rule)).
